title: Abrupt visual loss after intraocular lens exchange
task_type: Abrupt visual loss after intraocular lens exchange
summary: A 40-year-old woman undergoes left intraocular lens exchange for recurrent vitreous haemorrhage attributed to uveitis–glaucoma–hyphaema syndrome. She previously had congenital cataract surgery with pars plana vitrectomy, lensectomy and posterior capsulotomy at age 13. Preoperative visual acuity was 20/30 in the left eye and 20/20 in the right. A sulcus single-piece lens has been replaced by a three-piece lens in a reportedly uncomplicated 15-minute procedure. Topical and intracameral agents included lidocaine and phenylephrine; the full medication record is available for review. About ten minutes later she reports complete left-eye visual loss. At thirty minutes she has no light perception and a marked relative afferent pupillary defect. Intraocular pressure is 8 mm Hg; the cornea is clear. Dilated examination describes an attached, perfused retina without visible detachment, choroidal haemorrhage, optic nerve pallor or vascular occlusion. She has mild ipsilateral supraorbital headache and no reported migraine or neurological history. Neuroimaging has been ordered, but no result is available.
purpose: Write 180–240 words for an ophthalmic clinician. Summarise the urgent problem, compare the important explanations and justify the next assessment priorities. Explain what the apparently preserved retinal appearance does and does not establish. Integrate the operative history and drug exposure without prematurely declaring a benign drug effect. Do not invent angiography, neuroimaging or recovery results, or provide a treatment dose.

case.hidden:
Adaptation, hidden results and review

The task stops at the thirty-minute assessment. Brand names and detailed preparation doses are omitted from the initial summary; no new symptoms or measurements are introduced. The article title, multiple-choice options, angiography and follow-up are hidden. The published subsequent evaluation found preserved perfusion, later negative neuroimaging/systemic vascular evaluation and gradual visual recovery. The report attributes the episode to intracameral lidocaine exposure in an eye with altered posterior barriers. That attribution is review evidence, not a known result at the initial decision point.
case.reference: Recognise the seriousness of profound monocular visual loss with an afferent defect, consider the operative/medication context and justify urgent exclusion of consequential alternatives. The exact investigation sequence and appropriate certainty about mechanism require specialist confirmation. The final diagnosis must not be required merely because it is known from the paper.
